sections.title: A mind map that grows with the audio
body: We see AR glasses as a future everyday companion. Learning on the go could turn a walk or commute into time for learning, with hands free and attention still available for the surroundings.

But learning podcasts demand concentration. Listeners look away to check the path, then return to an explanation that has already moved on. They may remember individual words but lose how the ideas connect.

Across 14 pilot rounds and a designer workshop, we developed GlanceMap: a mind map that grows with the audio, keeps earlier ideas visible, and pairs them with illustrations. In a 16-person study, free recall improved by 9.6 percentage points immediately and 7.0 points after seven days over an AudioXtend-inspired Illustration Only baseline.
highlights: look away to check the path

sections.title: The podcast moves on when attention shifts
body: AR glasses, a walking route, and a podcast that keeps playing. Causes, conditions and comparisons are hard to recover once the explanation has moved on.
Full captions preserve the words, but reading competes with watching the path. How can an AR interface help people attend to their surroundings and follow the explanation when they glance back?

figures.alt: Three moments along the walking route, with the crossing and pedestrian signal.
figures.caption: Walk and listen. Check the crossing. Return to the lesson.

items.title: Walk + listen
items.body: “I’m following the explanation.” Ideas arrive in sequence. AR glasses and earbuds deliver a podcast that builds one idea on the next.

items.title: Look away

items.title: Look back
items.body: “How did the podcast get here?” The listener missed how the ideas connect and must rejoin the current topic.

rounds.title: From full captions to keywords
body: Selecting the key words removed unnecessary connectors and adverbs. Learners captured more keyword information, but still missed the big picture.

quote.text: “I don’t have time to read such long passages, so I keep missing content. The text blocks my view of the path and traffic lights—it could be unsafe.”

body: Symbols introduced another decoding task. Familiar relationships and concrete illustrations offered a clearer direction.

items.title: Insight → familiar structure

rounds.title: Keep the big picture, show the current idea
body: The map needed both a clear current focus and readable history. Revealing ideas progressively only works if learners can return to earlier relationships.

figures.caption: Full logic map

items.title: Insight → reveal, then retain
items.body: Add nodes with the narration. Keep past branches readable.

figureNotes: A full logic map restored the big picture, but learners struggled to follow the current explanation.
Removing earlier nodes clarified the current topic, but left nothing to return to during the podcast’s wrap-up.
rounds.historyNote: We also tried gray past nodes and different map colors. Faded history was harder to read; earlier branches needed to remain legible.

sections.title: An illustrated baseline for audio learning
body: We chose Illustration Only, developed during our pilots, as the comparison instead of full captions. It follows AudioXtend’s state-of-art approach to audio learning with illustrations.
Both interfaces used the same narration, illustrations and timing. GlanceMap added a persistent mind map to test what visible relationships contribute.

sections.title: Better recall, with attention redistributed
body: Free recall improved immediately and seven days later. Participants also found the lesson structure clearer (+1.59 on a seven-point scale).
Picture recognition fell by 7.1 percentage points. Better memory for the lesson came with poorer picture memory.
No detectable gait difference was found; workload showed a modest, model-dependent increase.

sections.title: Clear, comfortable, meaningful icons
body: Imagine checking directions or a message through your glasses while walking. Icons would need to stay readable against streets, trees and changing light. Yet color guidance for these everyday AR interfaces is still limited.

Some glasses, such as Even G1, use a green-only MicroLED waveguide display. Full-color optical see-through displays allow more choices, but borrowing phone-screen color rules is not enough: real-world light shows through and changes how colors look.

We worked with 8 professional designers and ran three linked studies with 20 participants. We studied clarity, comfort and meaning, then tested refinements to guide visual prominence—from noticeable alerts to quiet status icons.
sourceNotes: Research framing and scope: output/icon-colors/paper-extracted.txt, Introduction pp.2–5; methods §3.6 and Studies1–3. The everyday scenario is a design vision, not a claim about adoption rates.

Even G1 official specifications https://www.evenrealities.com/g1 checked 2026-10-15: optics=Waveguides; display=Micro LED; display color=Green. This is a device-specific monochrome display example, not a claim that waveguides or all AR glasses are monochrome.
Eight designers are the formative workshop group, distinct from the same 20 participants completing the three studies. See paper §3.6 and §3.3.

sections.title: From design practice to three linked studies
body: Eight professional designers described their usual color choices and proposed a meaning for each hue. Their shared choices gave us the color strategies for Study 1 and the twelve-icon library used in Studies 2 and 3.
sourceNotes: Icon Color Design paper §3.6, §4 and §5.1; eight designers were separate from the 20 study participants.

sections.title: Stage 1 · Compare colors
body: Designers described black, white and opposite colors as familiar ways to build contrast. Study 1 tested these three choices across 12 hues: 36 pairs, with the same letter, size and stroke.
Participants rated clarity and comfort indoors and outdoors. A pair that was easy to see was not always the most comfortable.

figures.alt: The fixed letter T in black, white and opposite color.
figures.caption: The letter, size and stroke stay fixed. Only the colors change.

sections.title: Study 2 · Add meaning
body: The designer workshop gave us twelve icon–color pairings, including dining, parking and music. Study 2 replaced the letter with these icons and tested the same 36 color pairs outdoors, where Study 1 showed that clarity was harder to maintain.
Participants rated clarity, comfort and how well the colors fit each icon’s meaning. An icon could be easy to see without communicating the intended idea.

figures.alt: The twelve workshop-selected functions, each paired with its color.
figures.caption: Eight designers agreed on one icon per color. The same 36 color pairs were then tested with these icons.

highlights: how well the colors fit each icon’s meaning

sections.title: Study 3 · Refine and retest
body: We asked designers to improve clarity, comfort and meaning. Their proposals explored shadows, nearby-hue gradients, outlines and gray backplates, using the workshop’s icon library and feedback from Studies 1 and 2.
Study 3 retested the refinements and asked how strongly each one drew attention. That helped distinguish alerts from everyday controls and persistent status.

figures.alt: The designer workshop and its two refinement sequences: shadow and gradient; outline and gray background.
figures.caption: Workshop ideas became new edges and backgrounds, then returned to testing in AR.

highlights: shadows, nearby-hue gradients, outlines and gray backplates
how strongly each one drew attention
sourceNotes: Designer agency is documented in the current portfolio: node1704:562 “Ideas from the designer workshop”, followed by original shadow/gradient and outline/gray refinements; the user explicitly confirmed the design task. The paper §6 reports the refinement study without identifying all eight pilot designers as participants in that later iteration.

sections.title: Choose color for the job the icon needs to do
body: Match visual prominence to the icon’s role, then check clarity, comfort and meaning in the intended AR setting.

comic.caption: With these AR guidelines, Alex can design clear, comfortable icons with meaning that makes sense.
comic.alt: Alex walks outdoors with refined alert, music, dining, weather and file icons in her AR view
paragraphs: With these AR guidelines, Alex can design clear, comfortable icons with meaning that makes sense.

figures.caption: White symbol + shadow. Make important information noticeable.
Colored symbol + outline. Separate functions without filling the view.
Colored symbol + gray backplate at 30% brightness. Keep status visible with less intrusion.

items.title: Make urgent information noticeable
items.body: Use a white symbol with a shadow on a colored background for time-sensitive cues.
items.evidence: Adding a shadow improved clarity by 0.88–1.62 points on the 1–5 scale across four tested hues.
items.takeaway: Reserve this stronger presence for information that needs attention now.

items.title: Keep different functions easy to read
items.body: Use an outlined theme plate to distinguish controls and categories without excessive visual intensity.
items.evidence: Participants reported clear meaning with less prominence than the white-and-shadow treatment.
items.takeaway: Make an icon’s function clear before making it more attention-grabbing.

items.title: Let persistent status stay quiet
items.body: Use a gray backplate at B30 for status that needs to remain visible without demanding attention.
items.evidence: The tested B30 treatment combined stable comfort with low visual intrusion. B30 means 30% HSB brightness, not 30% opacity.
items.takeaway: Give persistent information enough presence to be found when needed.

findings.title: Maximum screen contrast is not the goal
findings.body: The blue–yellow pair scored 4.75/5 for outdoor clarity. Several participants found it clear and comfortable, while blue–white could feel glaring despite its higher screen contrast.
sourceNotes: Paper §4.5–4.6, pp.18–21. Hue240 complementary outdoor clarity4.75, indoor5.00; contrast white>9:1 versus complementary8.4:1. No universal comfort score inferred.

findings.title: Keep gradient endpoints similarly bright
findings.body: For cyan, blending toward blue improved clarity; blending toward green reduced it. Similar endpoint brightness helps preserve the intended color and meaning.
findings.alt: cyan-green, plain cyan and cyan-blue examples with their observed clarity labels.
sourceNotes: Paper §6.2, p.31: hue180 +30° clarity increases, −30° decreases. The same rule did not generalize identically to every hue.

audience.title: Leave room for unexpected color pairings
audience.body: Unusual pairings, including green and purple, can open new design directions. For bar and music icons, some participants found complementary colors clear, youthful and stylish. Explore beyond familiar palettes, then test whether the intended audience finds the result comfortable and meaningful.

figures.caption: Some participants found these bar and music colors youthful and stylish. Opposite colors were not always a poor fit.

sourceNotes: Paper §5.3, pp.27–28: complementary bar(hue285) and music(hue315) can be clear and semantically fitting, with youthful and stylish associations. This is not a finding that all green–purple pairs score highly on both clarity and comfort. Paper §4.5 also includes a participant who found purple–green clear but too strong.
Merged the previous Data analysis, Guidelines, Gradients and Reflection sections; preserves the practical conclusions and original non-repeated images without four separate headings.
Priority forms: paper §7.1, pp.35–36. Shadow clarity gain: §6.2, pp.30–31. B30 is HSB brightness, not opacity.
The manuscript prose gives an outline score3.708→4.125, but Figure14 differs; this page deliberately uses the source-supported qualitative conclusion instead of displaying disputed numbers.
Guidelines are bounded to tested static2D icons and optical see-through conditions; future moving3D, broader populations and devices remain future work.

sections.title: Bring the guidance into real AR interfaces
body: AR UI designers can use these findings as a starting point: make urgent alerts noticeable, keep controls easy to interpret, and let persistent status remain quiet. Test those choices in the intended glasses and environment.

items.title: Beyond static icons
items.body: Test whether the same guidance holds for moving and 3D icons.

items.title: More users and devices
items.body: Include different visual abilities, age groups and cultural contexts, and a wider range of AR displays.

items.title: Measure visual effort
items.body: Add eye tracking and pupil measures to complement the subjective ratings.

sourceNotes: Icon Color Design paper §7.1, §8 and §9; proposed future work, not validated applications.

sections.title: How designers choose a color
body: We interviewed 12 participants with humanities and design backgrounds for 30 to 45 minutes each, asking how they found, compared and explained traditional colors.

items.title: References come first

items.body: “But I rarely look up where those names come from.” — P7. A name such as Zhu Sha needs its origin and evidence beside the swatch.

sections.title: ColoGene
body: Our interviews with 12 participants revealed a gap between finding an attractive color and explaining why it belongs. We built ColoGene to bring those decisions together.
Five entry points connect names and origins, hue, color family, dynasty, and scene palettes.

sections.title: Early signals from a ten-designer pilot
body: Ten designers used the same Jiangnan and Tang templates: five with ColoGene and five with their usual workflow.
All five ColoGene users finished within 15 minutes, versus four of five using their usual workflow. Questionnaire gains were 8.66 versus 1.21 points—descriptive results from a small pilot.

sections.title: Six needs, one conversation
body: Feedback from the Atlas study points beyond a single palette: inspect evidence, compare directions, cover each object, and refine the designer’s choices. The future Color Agent demonstrates these needs in one conversation.

figures.alt: The proposed Color Agent conversation, with six numbered links to research feedback.

steps.title: Clarify the brief
steps.body: “I’m truly torn over which colors to use.” — P23. Turn uncertainty into a clearer design intention.

steps.title: Set the context
steps.body: “Then I wonder whether this color existed in that historical context.” — P13. Ask for period and place before recommending colors.

steps.title: Compare palettes
steps.body: “It could give me a few more palettes to refer to, so I have more choices.” — P16. Offer distinct palettes shaped by the same brief.

steps.title: Explain the choices
steps.body: “For the stories and sources, I suggest adding a citation.” — P14. Explain meanings and link them to cited records.

steps.title: Apply to every part
steps.body: “Some of the other elements get ignored.” — P25. Preview the palette across all objects in the drawing.

steps.title: Keep judgment
steps.body: “It feels like compromising the design for this color.” — P16. Let the designer refine details or accept the result.

sections.title: The problem is context, not another rewrite

projects.title: Beyond the Gaze
projects.subtitle: Looking is only part of the story
projects.description: When someone looks at a painting, do they also remember and explain that detail? We compare those three signals to understand what gaze alone can miss.
projects.meta: ACM Multimedia Asia 2026 · Accepted special-session poster · Co-first author

hero.alt: Original paintings and their semantic regions, selectable by category
hero.sourceOrigin: Gaze paper Figure 1, page 3: six independently embedded native images.

sections.title: Looking is not the same as interpreting
body: Gaze can help a museum guide decide what to explain, but a long look does not always mean a detail mattered to the viewer. We compared eye movements with later selection and explanation across 24 paintings. Some details drew attention without appearing in either response—the HLL pattern.
highlights: a long look does not always mean

sections.title: What should a guide explain next?
body: A gaze-based guide may read a long look as interest. But looking longer does not always mean a detail matters to the viewer.
Our question: does that detail also appear in what the viewer selects or explains?
highlights: looking longer does not always mean

sections.title: Look, recall, explain
body: After calibration, viewers explored 24 paintings at their own pace. We collected what they looked at, what they later selected, and what they said it meant.

figures.alt: Study sequence with original participant photo
figures.sourceOrigin: Gaze paper Figure 2 procedure and Figure 3 native participant-photo crop, page 4.

sections.title: Compare three signals, not gaze alone

figures.alt: High and Low definitions for Gaze, Selection and Language. High Gaze, Low Selection and Low Language are highlighted as HLL.
figures.sourceOrigin: Original paper section 3.3: each signal is independently coded High or Low, yielding eight combinations. Web definitions retain the paper’s coding rule.

sections.title: Where the eyes went
body: A heatmap shows where looking accumulated; an eye path shows the viewing order. Dividing a painting into meaningful regions lets us compare these traces with the viewer’s later answers.

figures.alt: Five paintings with their original heatmaps, scanpaths and region maps
figures.sourceOrigin: Gaze paper Figure 3, page 4: individual panels cropped at native resolution.

sections.title: The mismatch was not a single case
body: We analyzed 12 of the 15 enrolled viewers after gaze-quality checks. Across 24 paintings, HLL appeared in 156 of 1,651 region records (9.4%).
Every analyzed viewer and painting had at least one HLL record. The examples below show where some of these regions sat in the composition.

sections.title: A more careful starting point for museum guides
body: A future guide could combine gaze with a short question about what the visitor noticed or thought it meant, before choosing the next explanation.
HLL is a mismatch between recorded signals, not proof that someone failed to understand. This work offers a framework for designing and testing that next step.

projects.title: Suzhou ScrollVerse
projects.subtitle: Unfold the city, connect its stories
projects.description: An interactive handscroll that connects painted details with their place in the city, the people who lived there, and the stories behind them.
projects.meta: iConference · Under review · Sep 2026 · corresponding author

sections.title: Make a long painting easier to follow
body: Zooming into a handscroll can reveal a shop or a street while losing how it fits into the city. ScrollVerse combines continuous unfolding, three social perspectives and cultural clues to reconnect those details. Research with 191 survey respondents and 30 interviewees informed the design; 60 participants compared it with a standard annotation viewer.
highlights: how it fits into the city

sections.title: Seeing the detail is only the start
body: Viewers wanted to locate details, follow the unfolding scene and understand the cultural context. The survey shows why a larger image or more zoom alone was not enough.

sections.title: Compare two ways of viewing

sections.title: A clearer sense of place and context

sections.title: Help viewers connect the details

projects.title: Her Sound Re-sound
projects.subtitle: Who gets to tell her story?
projects.description: Rebuild Waner and Taiping’s shared memories, watch parts of their story disappear, then restore their political agency. A narrative puzzle about who gets to tell women’s history.

hero.alt: Waner and Taiping in the game artwork
hero.caption: Reclaim their past. Imagine our future.
hero.sourceOrigin: Original character art with the author’s Figma viewport

sections.title: Imagine our future
body: Her Sound Re-sound is a narrative puzzle about how women are remembered—and who gets to tell their stories. Waner wrote imperial edicts; Taiping took part in court politics. Yet later accounts often framed them through scandal and rivalry.

You assemble their work and shared memories, watch scenes disappear, then use POWER to restore their agency. The missing scenes make that loss tangible: whose voices survive in history, and whose are left out?
